title: Brovada e Musetto
author: Marco Bellini
desc: A distinctive Friulian dish pairing a coarse pork sausage with fermented turnips, whose tangy, sour character comes from a lengthy marination in grape pomace left over from wine production.
longDesc: Brovada's unusual sour flavor comes from turnips fermented for weeks in the leftover skins and seeds from winemaking, a practical way to preserve the vegetable through winter that also produces a genuinely distinctive tang unlike anything else in Italian cooking.
ingredients: 1 musetto sausage (or a coarse pork sausage), about 500g/1.1lb
600 g (1.3 lb) brovada (fermented turnips) or substitute sauerkraut
steps: Prick the musetto sausage all over and simmer gently in water for about 1.5–2 hours until tender, following any specific package instructions.
Meanwhile, drain the brovada and rinse briefly if very sour.
Warm the lard or oil in a pan and sauté the onion until softened.
Add the brovada and cook over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 25–30 minutes until tender, adding a splash of water if it looks dry.
Season the brovada with salt and pepper.
Once the sausage is tender, remove and slice thickly.
Serve the sliced sausage alongside a generous portion of the brovada.
chefTips: True brovada, fermented in grape pomace, has a genuinely distinctive tang — sauerkraut is a reasonable but milder substitute if unavailable.
Follow specific cooking instructions for musetto sausage, as timing can vary by brand and size.
Rinse the brovada briefly before cooking if it tastes overwhelmingly sour for your preference.
commonMistakes: Overcooking the sausage until it splits and loses its texture.
Not cooking the brovada long enough, leaving it too raw and overly sharp in flavor.
Substituting a very different pickled vegetable without adjusting for the milder or sharper tang.
servedWith: A robust red wine from Friuli
healthBenefits: Fermented vegetables like brovada provide probiotics; a good source of protein from the sausage.
culturalNote: Brovada e musetto is a defining winter dish of Friuli, its fermented turnips a practical historical method for preserving vegetables through the cold months using leftover winemaking byproducts.
